source.title_on_document: Enhancing designer creativity through human–AI co-ideation: a co-creation framework for design ideation with custom GPT

supplement.holds: Examples of high and low rating scores for novelty, quality and variety in Supplementary Materials S1–S3 (p. 9, Idea assessment results); these separate materials were not read.

paper_design_summary: A preliminary survey asked 64 industrial design master students about challenges in their prior use of ChatGPT for ideation (pp. 3–4, Protocol and Results of study 1; Table 1). The validation experiment randomly divided 48 TU Delft master students into six groups crossing Co-Ideator versus no AI with trash can, alarm and kitchen blender design tasks (p. 8, Design study; Table 2). Researchers counted ideas, and raters with design experience scored the submitted ideas for novelty, quality/feasibility and variety within each participant’s ideas (p. 9, Idea assessment study; pp. 10 and 13, quantity Results and Discussion).

studies.label: Study 1: preliminary survey of ChatGPT ideation challenges

assignment.what_was_assigned: No experimental assistance conditions were described. Respondents were selected for prior ChatGPT ideation experience and completed the same survey; the assignment structure is not applicable.
assignment.quote: It is notable that when participants were selected, they were asked whether they had experience in co-generating ideas with ChatGPT.
assignment.locator: pp. 3–4, Protocol of study 1 (selection sentence on p. 4).

arms.name: Survey respondents
arms.description: Single survey sample with previous ChatGPT ideation experience; no AI intervention or comparison condition administered during the survey (pp. 3–4, Protocol of study 1; Table 1).

participants.who: Master students of industrial design with experience using ChatGPT for ideation. Table 1 gives a total of 64 respondents for each survey item.
participants.locator: pp. 3–4, Protocol of study 1; p. 4, Table 1 (survey denominator).

ai_tool.name_model: ChatGPT; model not stated for prior use
ai_tool.how_used: Prior ChatGPT ideation experience was elicited in a descriptive survey; no AI-assisted creative task was assigned (pp. 3–4, Protocol of study 1).

task.description: One-question survey about the major challenges encountered when using ChatGPT to generate ideas; no creative output was produced or scored (pp. 3–4, Protocol of study 1).

assignment.what_was_assigned: People were randomly divided among six groups crossing assistance (Co-Ideator or no AI) with design task (trash can, alarm or kitchen blender). Each person completed one task in one assistance condition.
assignment.quote: The 48 participants were equally divided into six groups at random (Table 2).
assignment.locator: p. 8, Design study; Table 2 maps the six groups to assistance and task.

arms.name: Co-Ideator
arms.description: Treatment groups 1–3, with eight people in each of the trash can, alarm and kitchen blender task cells (p. 8, Table 2); pooled assignment count is 8 + 8 + 8 = 24. The post-task treatment survey reports 24 responses (p. 14, Figure 12; also p. 12, novelty discussion).

arms.name: Without AI
arms.description: Control groups 4–6, with eight people in each of the trash can, alarm and kitchen blender task cells (p. 8, Table 2); pooled assignment count is 8 + 8 + 8 = 24. The post-task control survey reports 24 responses (p. 13, Figure 11).

participants.exclusions: Participant exclusions and the distinct number of people included in the idea-score tests are not separately reported (pp. 8–10, Participants, Design study and Idea assessment study/results).
participants.who: Master’s students of Industrial Design Engineering at Delft University of Technology, familiar with ChatGPT. The 48-person count is the recruited/randomized design sample (p. 8, Participants and Design study; Table 2). Figures 11 and 12 each show 24 post-task survey responses, not a separately reported analyzed-person count for the idea-score tests (pp. 13–14).
participants.quote: Forty-eight participants were recruited. All participants were master’s students of Industrial Design Engineering from the Delft University of Technology.
participants.locator: p. 8, Participants and Design study; Table 2; p. 13, Figure 11 (24 control responses); p. 14, Figure 12 (24 treatment responses).

ai_tool.name_model: Co-Ideator, a custom GPT powered by ChatGPT 4.0 (as named in the study protocol)
ai_tool.how_used: Participants entered the supplied design-challenge prompt and could then freely use the custom GPT. Its context-mapping instructions guided questions about present, past and future experiences; optional prompts requested elaboration, suggestions, alternative solutions and finalized ideas (p. 8, Design study; p. 9, Table 4).

task.description: Individually generate at least four ideas for one assigned product challenge: a trash can for student housing, a recyclable kitchen blender, or a multifunctional alarm for students. Submit each idea as a title and a description of around 40 words through an online survey; supporting paper sketches were not analyzed (p. 8, Design study; Table 3).

outcomes.name: Novelty of design ideas
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Three Strategic Product Design master students at TU Delft, each with at least four years of design experience, rated each idea on a 1–7 scale. Participant names were concealed and raters were blinded to assistance condition. Ratings were averaged across the three raters for each criterion (p. 9, Idea assessment study). Novelty measures originality/distinctiveness, from 1 = Overly explored to 7 = Never seen before (p. 9, Idea assessment study). Figure 8 labels this outcome Treatment Group N = 102 and Control Group N = 101; these are idea-score observations, not people (p. 10, Figure 8; labels visually checked). The Results instead report 102 treatment and 100 control ideas (p. 10, quantity paragraph), while the quantity Discussion reports 103 treatment and 100 control ideas (p. 13). n_units remains null because these counts conflict.

contrasts.reported: Co-Ideator mean rank = 110.28 versus without AI mean rank = 93.64; Mann–Whitney U = 4306.5, Z = −2.051, p = 0.040. These are the Results text values, corroborated in Discussion. The Figure 8 caption instead labels U = 2621.5, Z = −6.278, p < 0.001 as novelty; that caption conflicts with the Results and Discussion.
contrasts.locator: p. 10, Idea assessment results (novelty paragraph); p. 11, Discussion; p. 10, Figure 8 caption (conflicting labels); p. 9, Idea assessment study (rating definition and output unit). p. 8, Design study (conditions and output produced during the assigned session).

outcomes.name: Quality / feasibility of design ideas
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Three Strategic Product Design master students at TU Delft, each with at least four years of design experience, rated each idea on a 1–7 scale. Participant names were concealed and raters were blinded to assistance condition. Ratings were averaged across the three raters for each criterion (p. 9, Idea assessment study). Quality measures functional integrity and feasibility, from 1 = Not feasible at all to 7 = Easily realized (p. 9, Idea assessment study). Figure 8 labels this outcome Treatment Group N = 102 and Control Group N = 101; these are idea-score observations, not people (p. 10, Figure 8; labels visually checked). The Results instead report 102 treatment and 100 control ideas (p. 10, quantity paragraph), while the quantity Discussion reports 103 treatment and 100 control ideas (p. 13). n_units remains null because these counts conflict.

contrasts.reported: Co-Ideator mean rank = 126.80 versus without AI mean rank = 76.96; Mann–Whitney U = 2621.5, Z = −6.278, p < 0.001. These are the Results text values, corroborated in Discussion. The quality paragraph contains the word novelty in one sentence, but its question, conclusion and Discussion identify this as quality. The Figure 8 caption instead labels U = 4559.5, Z = −1.500, p = 0.133 as quality; that caption conflicts with the Results and Discussion.
contrasts.locator: p. 10, Idea assessment results (quality paragraph); p. 11, Discussion; p. 10, Figure 8 caption (conflicting labels); p. 9, Idea assessment study (quality defined as feasibility and output unit). p. 8, Design study (conditions and output produced during the assigned session).

outcomes.name: Variety within each participant’s design ideas
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Three Strategic Product Design master students at TU Delft, each with at least four years of design experience, rated each idea on a 1–7 scale. Participant names were concealed and raters were blinded to assistance condition. Ratings were averaged across the three raters for each criterion (p. 9, Idea assessment study). Variety concerns diversity among each participant’s own ideas, from 1 = Extremely limited to 7 = Highly diverse (p. 9, Idea assessment study; p. 13, variety Discussion). It is within-person flexibility; the stated per-idea scoring and averaging across raters support unit = output. Figure 8 labels this outcome Treatment Group N = 102 and Control Group N = 101; these are idea-score observations, not people (p. 10, Figure 8; labels visually checked). The Results instead report 102 treatment and 100 control ideas (p. 10, quantity paragraph), while the quantity Discussion reports 103 treatment and 100 control ideas (p. 13). n_units remains null because these counts conflict.

contrasts.reported: Co-Ideator mean rank = 107.80 versus without AI mean rank = 96.14; Mann–Whitney U = 4559.5, Z = −1.500, p = 0.133; no statistically significant difference. This measures variety among one participant’s own ideas, not similarity across different people. The methods say each idea was rated and the ratings were averaged across raters, so the recorded analysis unit is output.
contrasts.locator: p. 10, Idea assessment results (variety paragraph); p. 11, Discussion; p. 9, Idea assessment study (within-person variety definition and per-idea rating); p. 13, Impact of human–AI co-ideation on the variety of designers’ ideas. p. 8, Design study (conditions and output produced during the assigned session).

outcomes.name: Quantity of design ideas
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Researchers directly count the number of ideas per participant; quantity is not part of the raters’ assessment (p. 9, Idea assessment study). The reported statistics are totals for each assistance condition, so unit = set (p. 10, quantity Results; p. 13, quantity Discussion). The conflicting totals are preserved separately and n_units is left null. Ideas were produced in the assigned 30-minute session, with Co-Ideator available to the treatment arm and no AI in the control arm (p. 8, Design study).

contrasts.reported: Results: treatment total = 102 ideas; control total = 100 ideas (p. 10). Quantity Discussion: treatment total = 103 ideas; control total = 100 ideas (p. 13). The treatment totals conflict and neither is selected as definitive. The Discussion calls the difference almost negligible and not significant, but no numerical inferential test or uncertainty for quantity is printed. Only condition-level totals are reported; no effect size is derived. The Results state that quantity is not the core research focus.
contrasts.locator: p. 9, Idea assessment study (quantity definition); p. 10, Idea assessment results (quantity paragraph: 102 versus 100 and research priority); p. 13, Impact of human–-AI co-ideation on the quantity of designers’ ideas (103 versus 100 and qualitative conclusion); p. 8, Design study (conditions and timing).

eligibility.reason: Study 2 randomly assigned people to Co-Ideator versus no AI across six task/assistance cells (p. 8, Design study; Table 2) and scored their submitted ideas using raters with design experience (p. 9, Idea assessment study). Only 48 people were recruited/randomized, so the analyzed sample cannot reach the 50-person threshold even though its distinct-person count is not separately reported (pp. 8–10). The 24 responses in each post-task survey are survey denominators (p. 13, Figure 11; p. 14, Figure 12). Study 1 has 64 survey respondents but no assigned creative task or output-scored outcome (pp. 3–4, Protocol of study 1; Table 1); its sample cannot be added to Study 2. Under codebook section 3, this randomized experiment below the size threshold is excluded from core and is not observational context.

one_line_finding: In the experiment with 48 randomized people (p. 8), Co-Ideator ideas had higher novelty (U = 4306.5, p = 0.040) and quality/feasibility (U = 2621.5, p < 0.001), with no significant difference in within-person variety (U = 4559.5, p = 0.133; pp. 10–11, Results text and Discussion).
open_questions: How many distinct people contributed to the idea-score analyses in each arm, and were any participants excluded? The paper reports 48 recruited/randomized people and 24 responses per post-task survey, but no separate analyzed-person count (p. 8; p. 13, Figure 11; p. 14, Figure 12).

Which idea counts are correct? The Results report treatment/control totals of 102/100 (p. 10), Figure 8 labels every rated-outcome panel N = 102/101 (p. 10), and the quantity Discussion reports 103/100 (p. 13).
Can the conflicting novelty and quality test labels in the Figure 8 caption be corrected? The Results text and Discussion agree with each other (pp. 10–11).
notes: The complete 17-page markdown was read through the references; the PDF includes no appendices. Separate Supplementary Materials S1–S3 were not read. Recorded numbers were checked against the PDF, including visual checks of Figure 8, the negative Z statistics and Figures 11–12. Idea counts remain inconsistent: Results treatment/control = 102/100 (p. 10), Figure 8 rated-output N = 102/101 (p. 10), quantity Discussion = 103/100 (p. 13). No reconciled n_units is inferred. The Figure 8 caption conflicts with the Results and Discussion for novelty and quality; the Results quality paragraph also contains the stray word novelty. These conflicts are retained in the corresponding reported fields. Mean ranks are not raw arm means or standardized effects. The immediate outcomes were generated with AI available in the treatment arm; the control had no AI (p. 8, Design study).
